papers.title: Universality and Approximation Rates of Graph Neural Networks with Random Features
papers.rationale: A rigorous fixed-size GNN universality result that handles measurable invariant/equivariant functions and adds explicit depth/weight rates for smooth targets; highly relevant to approximation theory, with a clear boundary from size transfer.

report.executive_summary: This paper proves universal approximation and quantitative rates for permutation-equivariant neural networks (PENNs), a message-passing GNN class augmented with random node features. For directed graphs with a fixed number N of nodes, multidimensional node features, and multidimensional edge features, Theorem 9 states that any measurable permutation-equivariant target can be approximated in probability to arbitrary accuracy, provided the added random features give nodes unique identifiers with high probability (pp. 15-16). Invariant targets follow by repeating a graph-level value at every node and reading or averaging coordinates (Remark 13 and Corollary 14, p. 18). The architecture combines a local message-passing summary for each node with a global sum of transformed local summaries (Eqs. (4)-(5), pp. 15-16). Random identifiers break equivariance for a single realization, so the authors analyze averaging over independent feature draws: the conditional expectation is equivariant, Monte Carlo averages approach it, and the universality statement persists for any finite number of draws (Proposition 15 and Theorem 16, pp. 20-21). For k-times continuously differentiable targets on compact feature domains, Theorem 18 bounds each feedforward component's depth by O(log(1/epsilon)) and nonzero weights by O(epsilon^{-c_2/(k-1)} log^2(1/epsilon)) with high probability (pp. 23-25). This is a strong approximation-theory result but not a variable-size theorem: N is fixed and appears in constants and exponents. It gives no empirical experiments, and its use of random unique identifiers may be computationally expensive or statistically awkward, especially because averaging all permutations is infeasible.
report.why_it_fits: The paper matches the profile's interests in GNN expressivity, permutation invariance/equivariance, universal approximation, and quantitative mathematical guarantees. Its major added value over qualitative universality work is an explicit complexity rate for smooth targets. The distinction between measurable approximation in probability and uniform approximation on a compact domain is handled carefully, which aligns with the profile's preference for rigorous function-space statements. It also exposes a useful tension for any-dimensional research. Random identifiers can make fixed-N message passing universal, but the construction depends on N and sacrifices realization-wise equivariance; therefore it does not automatically define one coherent model across sizes. This makes the paper a valuable negative/contrast case for size transfer: expressivity obtained by individualizing nodes may conflict with dimension-independent consistency. Pairing the result with graphon or manifold limit theory could clarify which symmetry-breaking features vanish, stabilize, or admit exchangeable couplings as N changes. The averaging argument may also connect to randomized equivariant architectures and to RPEARL-style random encodings in the leading paper, though the assumptions and goals differ.
report.problem_formulation: The graph domain D_{N,d,d'} contains directed graphs with exactly N nodes, node features in R^d, and edge features in R^{d'}. The symmetric group S_N permutes node and adjacency tensors. A PENN computes, for each node k, a local aggregate over incoming neighbors and a global aggregate over all nodes; its component maps rho, phi, alpha, and psi are feedforward networks (Definition 1 and Eq. (5), pp. 6 and 16). Random features R in R^{N x d_r} are concatenated to node features. The essential condition is finite unique node features: with high probability a measurable hashing map assigns different labels to every node (Definition 3, pp. 10-11). The qualitative question is whether this augmented PENN approximates any measurable equivariant or invariant f in probability under a graph distribution. The quantitative question restricts node/edge features to [0,1], assumes f is k-times continuously differentiable with derivatives bounded by kappa, and asks how component-network depth and sparsity scale with epsilon and confidence delta (Eq. (7) and Theorem 18, pp. 22-23).
contributions: A universality theorem for measurable permutation-equivariant functions on fixed-size directed attributed graphs using PENNs with partially random node features (Theorem 9, pp. 15-16).

Extensions to probability measures already inducing unique node features, uniform approximation for continuous targets under finite-support unique identifiers, and invariant graph outputs (Theorem 11, Corollaries 12 and 14, pp. 16-18).
An analysis of permutation equivariance in expectation and Monte Carlo feature averaging that preserves approximation power (Proposition 15 and Theorem 16, pp. 20-21).
Explicit ReLU component complexity bounds for smooth equivariant/invariant functions, separating logarithmic depth from polynomial weight growth (Theorem 18, pp. 23-25).
Expressivity examples explaining why random identifiers distinguish graphs beyond ordinary message-passing limitations (Appendix E, Figures 1-3).
report.method: Unique random node features let the authors encode a canonical node-specific description within a permutation-equivariant aggregate-and-combine template. A representation proposition first shows that on any set of graphs with finite unique node features, a measurable equivariant target can be expressed using four measurable local/global component functions. A neural approximation proposition then approximates these measurable components under the pushforward input distribution. Intersecting the high-probability uniqueness event with the component approximation event proves Theorem 9. For compact continuous targets with random permutations of deterministic distinct identifiers, the component functions can be replaced by continuous extensions and uniformly approximated. The equivariance-in-expectation result uses a permutation-invariant feature distribution and independence from the graph to commute conditional expectation with permutation. Quantitative rates discretize the identifier interval into bins, construct smooth component representations away from bin boundaries, control the probability of collisions/boundary events, and apply known ReLU approximation rates for smooth functions. The resulting exponent c_2 depends on graph size and input dimensions, while higher regularity k improves the epsilon exponent. The probability statement has two logically separate sources: random identifiers must avoid collisions and bad bin boundaries, and the component networks must approximate the constructed representation. Corollary 19 shows that random permutations of a fixed set of N distinct identifiers can make the rate statement sure rather than merely high probability. This strengthens approximation but makes the dependence on fixed N even more explicit. The Monte Carlo averaging theorem does not give a finite-M equivariance-error rate; it preserves target approximation for any M while the law of large numbers motivates equivariance improvement as M grows (Section 4.2, pp. 19-21).

papers.title: A New Convergence Analysis of Plug-and-Play Proximal Gradient Descent Under Prior Mismatch
papers.rationale: A distinct secondary-lane match: nonconvex plug-and-play convergence under prior mismatch, with an explicit equivariant group-averaging improvement in the error term.

report.executive_summary: This paper gives a convergence analysis for plug-and-play proximal gradient descent (PnP-PGD) when the deployed denoiser is trained on a distribution different from the target prior. It interprets a gradient-step MMSE denoiser as the proximal map of a possibly nonconvex regularizer and treats the mismatched denoiser as an inexact proximal step. Under Lipschitz-gradient and bounded-below assumptions, equality of target and mismatched denoiser ranges, and an epsilon_k-optimality condition, Theorem 2.1 bounds the average squared stationarity measure by an O(1/t) objective-gap term plus an averaged cumulative mismatch error (Eq. (14), p. 5). If the epsilon_k sequence is summable, the gradient of the target objective converges to zero. The analysis allows nonconvex data fidelities and regularizers and expansive denoisers; it avoids bounded-iterate assumptions used by some prior mismatch analyses (Table 1 and Section 2, pp. 2-4). The paper then models structural mismatch as anisotropic denoiser bias and group-averages transformed denoiser outputs. Under invariant target density and isotropic Gaussian noise, the target denoiser is equivariant. Jensen-style strict bias reduction yields a smaller error term when the bias varies across group actions (Lemma 2.2, Eq. (17), p. 7), and Theorem 2.3 substitutes that reduced term into the PnP convergence bound (Eq. (20), pp. 7-8). The work is entirely theoretical: there are no inverse-problem experiments, learned denoisers, or numerical estimates of mismatch errors. Several assumptions remain difficult to verify, especially equal denoiser ranges and per-iteration epsilon-optimality relative to the unknown target prior.
report.why_it_fits: This is a secondary but meaningful fit to the profile's interests in learned proximal methods, inverse problems, nonconvex optimization, and equivariant architectures. It provides a bridge between two lanes that are often treated separately: convergence of learned proximal algorithms and symmetry-based bias reduction. The stationarity guarantee is explicit about how prior mismatch accumulates, making it potentially useful for comparing proximal matching or denoiser-regularized approaches. The group-averaging argument also turns equivariance into a quantitative improvement in an optimization bound rather than only an expressivity or sample-efficiency principle. However, the fit is below the three theory papers because it does not address variable-size learning, limit spaces, or universality, and it lacks experiments. Its assumptions should be viewed as a starting point for stronger, observable mismatch conditions rather than a complete operational guarantee.
report.problem_formulation: The target inverse problem minimizes F_{lambda,sigma}(x)=lambda f(x)+phi_sigma(x), where f is differentiable and phi_sigma is the regularizer whose proximal map equals a target gradient-step denoiser D_sigma (Eqs. (6)-(10), pp. 3-4). In deployment, D_sigma is replaced by a mismatched MMSE denoiser Dhat_sigma trained under another prior. Each mismatched output must be an epsilon_{k+1}-optimal solution of the target proximal subproblem (Assumption 2.5, Eq. (11), p. 4), equivalently controlling its distance to the target denoiser via Eq. (13). The aim is to bound stationarity of F under PnP-PGD iterates. For the equivariant extension, the ideal density is invariant under affine transformations with isometric linear parts and observation noise is isotropic. The deployed denoiser has bias E relative to the ideal one; averaging inverse-transformed denoiser outputs over the group produces an equivariant denoiser whose anisotropic bias is smaller.
contributions: A PnP-PGD stationarity bound under mismatched MMSE denoisers without bounded-iterate assumptions (Theorem 2.1, Eq. (14), p. 5).
Coverage of nonconvex fidelity/regularization and potentially expansive denoisers through the gradient-step/proximal characterization (Proposition 2.1 and Assumptions 2.1-2.3, pp. 3-4).
A structural-prior-mismatch interpretation connecting architectural bias with transformation groups (Section 2.3, pp. 5-6).
A strict reduction of anisotropic denoiser bias by equivariant group averaging (Lemma 2.2, Eq. (17), p. 7).
An EPnP-PGD convergence bound in which the mismatch term is tightened by the variance across group actions (Theorem 2.3, Eq. (20), pp. 7-8).
report.method: A gradient-step denoiser D=Id-grad g with Lipschitz residual smaller than one is represented as a proximal operator of a smooth, possibly nonconvex phi. The mismatched denoiser output is analyzed as an inexact solution to this target proximal step. Descent inequalities relate the change in F to step norms and epsilon_k; Lipschitz properties then convert step control into a stationarity bound. Summing and telescoping over t iterations produces Eq. (14), and summability of epsilon_k forces stationarity. For equivariant PnP, invariance of the target prior and isotropic noise imply equivariance of the MMSE target denoiser. Conjugating the mismatched denoiser by a sampled group transformation and averaging preserves the target component while averaging its bias. Strict convexity of the squared norm/Jensen reasoning makes the averaged anisotropic bias smaller than the average original bias. The paper defines the resulting reduction as a variance gain and inserts the smaller error sequence into the same telescoping convergence proof. A useful detail is that the denoiser itself need not be nonexpansive. The authors require the residual Id-D to be contractive; if its Lipschitz constant exceeds one, they propose relaxing the denoiser through D_alpha=alpha D+(1-alpha)Id with alpha small enough (Assumption 2.2 discussion, p. 4). Proposition 2.1 then supplies injectivity and a smooth implicit regularizer whose gradient has controlled Lipschitz constant. The matched-denoiser special case removes all epsilon terms and improves the leading constant from 16 to 8 (Theorem 2.2, Eq. (15), p. 5), helping isolate the price assigned to mismatch by this analysis. The group-averaged error is written as the average error minus a variance gain, so strict improvement disappears when the bias is already isotropic across transformations. The result therefore distinguishes symmetry-compatible systematic bias from arbitrary mismatch rather than claiming that averaging always improves every denoiser.

papers.title: Optimal Symmetries in Binary Classification
papers.rationale: A diverse symmetry-design result: it connects optimal classification to likelihood-ratio fibres and shows theoretically and empirically why imposing a larger group than the task supports can hurt.

report.executive_summary: This paper studies how to choose a symmetry group for binary classification rather than assuming that the largest available group gives the best inductive bias. Starting from Neyman-Pearson optimality, an optimal score must be a monotone function of the likelihood ratio P_1/P_0, so its level sets—or fibres—must match those of that ratio (Observation 1, p. 5). Group-invariant functions are constant on group orbits, and equivariant maps identify at least those points connected by stabilizer elements of the output (Observations 2-3 and Eqs. (3)-(7), pp. 5-6). The authors define input/output group actions as optimal when the corresponding equivariant function class contains a map with the likelihood ratio's fibre decomposition (Definition 9, p. 6). For invariant classifiers this gives a crisp condition: a group action is optimal if and only if the likelihood ratio is invariant under it (Observation 4, p. 6). A subgroup of a valid invariant group remains valid but may use fewer equivalences and therefore less sample efficiency; a strictly larger group can merge likelihood-ratio fibres and make optimal classification impossible. The equivariant case depends additionally on the hidden representation's group action, and the strongest claims there are presented partly as a conjectural extension. Synthetic point-cloud experiments compare E(3), O(3), and O(2) invariant/equivariant networks on sphere-versus-cylinder tasks. O(2), the symmetry shared by the likelihood ratio, achieves essentially perfect background rejection with both 10k and 100k samples per class, whereas larger groups perform worse, especially for invariant models (Tables 1-2, p. 9). The result is conceptually useful but narrow: binary classification, known class distributions/symmetries, simple 3D experiments, and no general learning bound.
report.why_it_fits: The paper fits the profile's strong interest in invariant/equivariant architectures and adds a design perspective not covered by the universality selection. Universality asks whether a model spans all functions compatible with an imposed group; this paper asks whether the imposed group is compatible with the statistically optimal target in the first place. Its fibre formulation connects group orbits, stabilizers, and likelihood-ratio level sets in a way that could inform representation selection. This is especially relevant when building any-dimensional or scientific models where abundant physical symmetries tempt designers to impose overly large groups. The paper's warning is precise: a larger group can improve sample efficiency only if it does not collapse target-relevant distinctions. The fit is lower than the newer theory papers because the work sits just inside the two-year window, focuses on binary classification, and leaves parts of the equivariant extension informal. Still, it provides empirical evidence and a clear counterweight to blanket claims that more symmetry is always better.
report.problem_formulation: Data X come from either P_0 or P_1 on a shared domain D, and a scalar classifier threshold defines false-positive rate epsilon_0 and true-positive rate epsilon_1 (Section 3, pp. 4-5). Neyman-Pearson theory makes monotone transformations of lambda(X)=P_1(X)/P_0(X) optimal across thresholds. A group G acts on input space X and hidden/output space H. Invariant functions are constant along G-orbits; equivariant functions map input transformations through an output action, so stabilizers determine subsets that must share a fibre (Section 4, Eqs. (3)-(7), pp. 5-6). The selection problem is to choose input and output group actions whose forced fibres do not merge distinct likelihood-ratio fibres. For invariant classifiers, this reduces to requiring lambda to be G-invariant. For equivariant feature extractors, optimality also depends on the hidden action and whether stabilizer-induced fibres respect lambda.
contributions: A Neyman-Pearson formulation of symmetry selection in terms of likelihood-ratio fibre decompositions (Observation 1, p. 5).
Orbit- and stabilizer-based lower bounds on fibres of invariant and equivariant maps (Observations 2-3, Eqs. (3)-(7), pp. 5-6).
A definition of an optimal pair of input/output group actions for binary classification (Definition 9, p. 6).
A necessary-and-sufficient condition for invariant symmetry optimality: invariance of the likelihood ratio (Observation 4, p. 6).
Synthetic 3D point-cloud evidence that the task-appropriate O(2) group outperforms larger O(3) and E(3) choices (Section 6, Tables 1-2, pp. 8-9).
report.method: The theoretical argument first translates ROC optimality into a geometric condition on classifier fibres. It then studies which equalities are forced by group actions. For invariant maps, every orbit lies inside one fibre. For equivariant maps, the subset of an orbit reached by elements stabilizing the output must lie in one fibre. Comparing these minimal fibres with likelihood-ratio fibres yields the definition of optimal symmetry. In the invariant case, the likelihood ratio being G-invariant is both necessary and sufficient. If only a subgroup preserves it, imposing a larger group destroys optimality by merging target-distinct points. The experiments generate 30-point clouds from spheres and cylinders, add Gaussian coordinate noise with standard deviation corresponding to diagonal covariance 0.3, and train architectures based on classical-group equivariant layers. They compare invariant and equivariant E(3), O(3), and axis-aligned O(2) models at two training-set sizes over ten initializations, evaluating validation loss and background rejection at 95% signal acceptance. The subgroup argument has an important asymmetry. If G is a valid invariant symmetry, restricting to a proper subgroup G' remains capable of representing the likelihood ratio because it forces fewer identifications, but it may sacrifice sample efficiency by creating smaller orbits. Enlarging beyond the invariance group can instead be irrecoverably harmful because every invariant function must identify points whose likelihood ratios differ. For equivariant feature extraction, the output action changes stabilizers and hence changes the forced fibres; choosing only an input group is therefore insufficient. The paper argues that larger-group equivariance can remain useful if hidden actions are engineered to be trivial on target-preserving subgroups, but it defers a fully general theorem for this case (Section 5.2, pp. 7-8).

report.experiments: Two synthetic tasks classify 30-point clouds sampled from a sphere versus a cylinder. The uniform task uses unit-radius shapes; the truncated-normal task makes probability symmetry, rather than only support, decisive. Gaussian coordinate noise is added, and training uses 10k or 100k samples per class with ten random initializations (Section 6, p. 8). At 95% signal acceptance, O(2) invariant and equivariant models achieve 1.000 background rejection on the uniform task at both data sizes. O(3) invariant rises from 0.864 to 0.905 and E(3) invariant from 0.853 to 0.868; equivariant larger groups improve but remain below O(2) (Table 1, p. 9). On the harder truncated-normal task, O(2) remains about 0.998-0.999, O(3) about 0.988-0.995, and E(3) invariant is only 0.331 at 10k and 0.652 at 100k (Table 2, p. 9). The results support the claim that a correct smaller group can be both more accurate and more sample-efficient, but they cover only simple synthetic geometry and do not isolate architecture capacity across groups.
limitations: The formal optimality result is for binary classification with likelihood-ratio structure; multiclass and regression extensions are absent.
Task symmetries of P_0 and P_1 are assumed known, whereas real distributions are only observed through samples.
The equivariant hidden-representation discussion includes conjectural elements and is less complete than the invariant criterion.
Experiments use only synthetic sphere/cylinder point clouds and three classical groups.
No generalization bound quantifies gains or penalties from symmetry mismatch.
report.reproducibility: The paper specifies distributions, point count, noise level, training-set sizes, groups, repetition count, and evaluation metric; supplementary material contains architecture details. The report used the arXiv v1 PDF dated 16 August 2024. Exact optimizer settings, seeds, and code availability were not identified in the inspected main text, so numerical replication requires consulting the supplement and repository metadata.
research_ideas: Estimate likelihood-ratio fibre compatibility from data to choose groups adaptively rather than from known distributions.
Extend optimal-symmetry criteria to multiclass sufficient statistics and equivariant regression.

Study approximate symmetries and bound excess risk caused by orbit-wise variation of the likelihood ratio.
Test subgroup selection in variable-size scientific datasets where symmetry and discretization refinement interact.
warnings: The paper is near the lower boundary of the two-year scan window.
The largest-group-is-worse conclusion is task-dependent, not a universal rejection of larger symmetries.
Some equivariant claims are motivated as conjectural rather than fully proved.
